# Analysis of the HRM Thinker training run (24 h model, step 4,050)

## In one paragraph: what we built and whether it worked

You built a small language model, 25 million working parameters, and trained it for 22 hours on a MacBook Air. It has an unusual design. The part that writes each word (the *decoder*) can only see the last 70 tokens. A token is a word or a piece of a word. Anything older has to reach the decoder through a compressed "plan". A *concept module* builds that plan by squeezing every 4 tokens into one summary, called a *concept*. The central idea worked. The model can answer questions whose answers sit 128–420 tokens back, well past what the decoder can see. When the plan is removed, that ability disappears. Everyday text prediction improved steadily with no instability. Three things are still weak: harder multi-step reasoning, the "think longer" loop (it adds nothing measurable), and performance on longer-than-trained inputs.

## What we achieved (the evidence)

- **Long-range memory works through the plan.** On the test set, simple recall scores 0.971 exact match. With the concept module off it drops to 0.004. With another example's plan swapped in it also drops to 0.004. The answer can only travel through the plan.
- **It partly works on longer inputs.** On inputs about twice as long as in training, recall still scores 0.801.
- **Language got much better.** The average validation loss (lower is better) fell from 5.089 to 2.754. On TinyStories the final test loss is 1.977 nats (0.724 bits per byte). On WikiText, which is harder, it is 3.629 nats (1.450 bits per byte).
- **The model depends heavily on the concept path.** Turning off the concept module raises TinyStories loss from 1.977 to 2.555. On WikiText it goes from 3.629 to 4.084.
- **Training was stable.** The gradient norm (how hard each update pushes) stayed at 0.32–0.38. There were 0 safety-guard events.
- **The design rules hold on the trained weights.** All 3 exact structural tests passed. The model cannot see the future. The decoder's reach is exactly 70 tokens. Separate documents do not leak into each other.
- **The codebook is healthy.** The codebook is the fixed "dictionary" of codes used to describe concepts. Every one of its 6,144 codes is used. Average usage spread is 108.5 out of 128.
- **Simple structured tasks are strong.** sort_trace scores 1.00, nested_scopes 0.99, json_build 0.98, seq_transform 0.97 and brackets 0.94.
- **The writing is fluent.** The TinyStories sample reads naturally. It has one slip: the girl's name changes from Polly to Mandy.

## What did not work or is still weak

- **Four-step carrying (multi4) is far below target.** It scores 0.082 against the 0.5 target. Per-token credit is 0.76–0.82, so most pieces come out right but the whole answer rarely does.
- **Multi-hop and binding are weak.** hop scores 0.092. bind scores 0.029, which is *lower* than with concepts off (0.049). In other words, bind has not been learned at all.
- **Longer-than-trained inputs are the biggest gap.** The synthetic-task average falls from 0.554 on test to 0.221 on longer inputs. Several tasks collapse completely: brackets goes from 0.94 to 0.00, nested_scopes from 0.99 to 0.00, and stack_ops from 0.84 to 0.00.
- **Chain-following tasks are near zero.** pointer_chase scores 0.06 and graph_walk 0.09.
- **Concepts are not exact copies of their tokens.** A simple probe can recover a concept's 4 tokens only 0.63–0.70 of the time. The target was 0.99. That is still about 14× better than the ~0.05 baseline.
- **Distant text helps only a little.** On WikiText, seeing 1,024 tokens instead of 72 improves loss by just 0.040 nats.

## Surprises and interesting observations

- **Abilities switched on in order.** Recall sat near 0 until step 766. It then jumped to 0.117, 0.336, 0.477 and on to 0.98. Carrying (carry3) started around step 2,190 and was still rising at the end (0.594–0.617). multi4 only began to move around step 3,121. It may simply be early.
- **The "think longer" loop does nothing measurable.** Running the loop 1, 2, 4 or 8 times gives almost identical TinyStories loss (1.9767–1.9780). On the probes, one pass is as good as four (carry3: 0.596 with one pass vs 0.580 with four). The angle between successive loop steps shrinks from 6.70° to 0.11°. That means later passes keep pushing in the same direction and add nothing new. Yet switching the loop state off entirely hurts a lot (1.977 → 2.488). The loop is useful as a layer, but repeating it is not.
- **A wrong plan hurts much more than distant text helps.** On TinyStories a swapped plan costs about 0.9 nats. Everything beyond 70 tokens gains only 0.076. So the plan must also carry *nearby* information that the decoder relies on. Caveat: only 1 of 256 TinyStories test rows had 512 or more tokens of context, so this number rests on short stories.
- **Concepts come almost entirely from the global stream (0.84 share).** The memory table (*Engram*) gate is 0.806 open, so the model uses it a lot. We have no test yet of what it contributes.
- **Some results look odd but are probably noise.** copy scores higher on longer inputs (0.54) than on test (0.48), and so does yaml_lookup (0.23 vs 0.20). Treat both as noise until checked.

## How it compares to what we expected (the pre-registered gates)

"Pre-registered" means these pass/fail targets were written down before looking at the results.

| Gate | Plain meaning | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Screen gate | Limited decoder no worse than a normal one | PASS (4.341 vs 4.351; the difference is tiny and likely noise) |
| G-E0/D0 | Structural rules hold exactly | PASS |
| G-E1 | A concept holds its 4 tokens almost perfectly (≥0.99) | NOT MET (0.63–0.70) |
| G-E2 | Concepts keep ≥60% of the information (variance explained) | PASS (0.651) |
| G-C1 | ≥95% of dictionary codes used | PASS (100%) |
| G-C2 | Next concept is predictable | PASS (loss 2.698 < entropy 4.686) |
| G-E3/D2 | Wrong plan → chance-level answers, and plan use matches long-range gain | PARTLY (the first half holds; the plan costs far more than distance gains) |
| G-C3 | 4 loop passes beat 1 on multi-hop | WITHIN NOISE (3 items out of 512, z = 0.33) |
| G-D3 | multi4 ≥ 0.5 | NOT MET (0.08) |

## What the running +24 h continuation is testing and what to watch for

The continuation adds another ~24 h of training on new rows, running to step 8,100. The learning rate (step size) first climbs back up to 6e-4 and then slowly winds down again. It tests three things:

1. Does more data keep lowering loss? A fitted curve predicts about 2.53 final validation, down from 2.754.
2. Does carry3 keep climbing, and does multi4 finally take off?
3. Does the model keep what it already learned?

What to watch:

- **A temporary rise is expected.** Validation should go up by +0.10 to +0.15, then drop back below 2.754 about 1,500 steps in. About 0.2 nats of the first run's late gains came from the slow wind-down, so this early rise is normal and not a failure.
- **The model is still in the warm-up.** Right now it is at step 4,100, train loss 2.096 (vs 2.085 before), learning rate 1.5e-4. There is no validation eval yet.
- **Warning signs:**
  - the rise goes above ~0.15 or does not recover by ~1,500 steps in
  - recall drops clearly below ~0.95
  - codebook use or variance explained falls
  - any safety-guard event, or the gradient norm leaves 0.32–0.38
- **Judge it at step 8,100.** Mid-run numbers will look worse by design.

## Recommended next steps (ranked)

1. **Let the continuation finish, and check the warning signs above at each hourly eval.**
2. **Settle the loop question.** One pass matches four everywhere. Either drop the extra passes and save compute, or train on tasks that force several steps. Use larger probe sets so the gate can actually be decided.
3. **Debug bind.** Scoring below the concepts-off version suggests the task or its scoring may be broken, not just hard.
4. **Train on mixed lengths** to fix the collapse on longer inputs (brackets, stack_ops, nested_scopes).
5. **Revisit the G-E1 target.** 0.99 may be unrealistic for a summary. Decide whether concepts should store meaning or exact tokens.
6. **Measure what Engram is worth.** It holds 50 million of the 78.6 million stored parameters, and we have no test of its value yet.

## Glossary

- **Token**: a word or word-piece the model reads and writes.
- **Nats / bits per byte (bpb)**: units of prediction error. Lower is better.
- **Validation / test set**: held-out text the model never trained on.
- **Decoder**: the part that writes each next token.
- **Concept**: one summary vector made from 4 tokens.
- **Plan**: the concept information passed to the decoder.
- **Codebook / product quantisation**: describing each concept with codes picked from 48 small dictionaries.
- **VQ loss**: the training penalty that keeps concepts close to their codes.
- **Loop (R)**: repeating one layer several times to "think longer".
- **Ablation**: switching a part off to see how much it matters.
- **Probe task**: a small synthetic test such as recall or carry.
- **Exact match**: the answer counts only if it is fully correct.
- **OOD**: inputs unlike training, here about 2× longer.
- **Linear probe**: a very simple reader that tests what information a vector holds.
- **Variance explained**: the share of information kept after compression.
- **Perplexity (of a codebook)**: how many codes are effectively in use.
- **Entropy**: how unpredictable something is.
- **Engram**: a large lookup table of short word patterns.
- **Learning rate / warm-up / cosine / annealing**: the update step size, ramping it up, then smoothly lowering it.
- **Gradient norm**: how big each training update is.
- **Epoch**: one full pass over the data.
- **z-score**: how far a difference is from noise. Below ~2 means likely noise.
- **Pre-registered gate**: a pass/fail target fixed before seeing results.

HARDWARE/DATA: Apple M2 MacBook Air 16 GB (MPS, float32), 32,768 tokens per step, data mix: language 45% (TinyStories + WikiText-103), symbolic 22%, retrieval 13%, code 10%, synthetic long-range probes 10% (answers 128-420 tokens back, beyond the decoder's reach).
